title: Chapter XXXI
paragraphs: Yesterday was clear, still, and frosty. I went to the Heights as planned. My housekeeper begged me to carry a short note to her young mistress, and I agreed, since the good woman saw nothing odd in the request. The front door stood open, but the unwelcoming gate was locked, as on my previous visit. I knocked, calling Earnshaw away from the garden beds. He unfastened the chain and let me in. The fellow is as handsome a countryman as one could wish to see. I noticed him particularly this time, though he seems determined to make as little as possible of his advantages.

I asked whether Mr. Heathcliff was home. He said no, but he would return for dinner. It was eleven o’clock. When I said I would go in and wait, he immediately put down his tools and came with me, acting as a watchdog rather than a substitute host.

We went in together. Catherine was there, making herself useful by preparing vegetables for the coming meal. She looked sulkier and less spirited than when I first saw her. She barely raised her eyes at my arrival and continued her task with the same disregard for ordinary politeness as before, offering not the slightest acknowledgment of my bow or good morning.
“She doesn’t seem as pleasant as Mrs. Dean would have me believe,” I thought. “A beauty, certainly, but no angel.”

Earnshaw gruffly told her to take her things into the kitchen. “Take them yourself,” she said, pushing them away as soon as she had finished. She withdrew to a stool by the window and began cutting shapes of birds and animals from the turnip peelings in her lap. Pretending I wanted to look at the garden, I approached and, very deftly I thought, dropped Mrs. Dean’s note onto her knee without Hareton noticing. But she asked aloud, “What’s that?” and tossed it off.

“A letter from your old friend, the housekeeper at the Grange,” I answered, annoyed that she had exposed my kindness and afraid it might be mistaken for a message of my own. On hearing this she would gladly have picked it up, but Hareton was quicker. He snatched it and put it inside his waistcoat, saying Mr. Heathcliff must see it first. Catherine silently turned away from us, slipped out her handkerchief as secretly as she could, and put it to her eyes. For a while her cousin struggled to suppress his softer feelings, then pulled out the letter and threw it on the floor beside her as ungraciously as possible. Catherine seized it and read it eagerly. She asked me a few questions about the inhabitants of her former home, human and animal, then looked towards the hills and murmured to herself:

“I wish I could ride Minny down there! I wish I could climb up there! Oh! I’m tired—I’m _fed up_, Hareton!” She leaned her pretty head against the sill with a sound halfway between a yawn and a sigh, and sank into an absent sadness, neither knowing nor caring whether we noticed her.

“Mrs. Heathcliff,” I said after sitting silently for some time, “do you realise that I know you? So well, in fact, that I’m surprised you won’t come and talk to me. My housekeeper never tires of talking about you and singing your praises. She’ll be terribly disappointed if I bring back no news of you, or message from you, beyond saying that you received her letter and said nothing!”
She seemed surprised by this speech and asked—
“Does Ellen like you?”
“Yes, very much,” I answered, with some hesitation.
“Then tell her,” she continued, “that I’d answer her letter, but I’ve nothing to write with or on. Not even a book I could tear a page from.”
“No books!” I exclaimed. “If I may ask, how do you manage to live here without them? Even with a large library, I’m often terribly bored at the Grange. Take my books away and I’d be desperate!”

“When I had them, I was always reading,” Catherine said. “Mr. Heathcliff never reads, so he took it into his head to destroy my books. I haven’t seen one for weeks. Once I searched through Joseph’s stock of theology, which made him furious. And once, Hareton, I found a secret collection in your room: Latin and Greek, stories and poetry, all old friends. The stories and poems were ones I’d brought here. You collected them like a magpie collecting silver spoons, simply for the pleasure of stealing! They’re no use to you. Or perhaps you hid them out of spite: if you can’t enjoy them, nobody else shall. Perhaps it was _your_ envy that suggested Mr. Heathcliff should rob me of my treasures? But most of them are written in my mind and printed on my heart, and you can’t take those away!”
Earnshaw went crimson as his cousin exposed his private collection of books and stammered an indignant denial of her charges.
“Mr. Hareton wishes to improve his knowledge,” I said, coming to his aid. “He doesn’t _envy_ your accomplishments; he wants to _equal_ them. In a few years he’ll be a fine scholar.”

“And meanwhile he wants me to become a dunce,” Catherine replied. “Yes, I hear him trying to spell and read to himself. What fine mistakes he makes! I wish you’d repeat Chevy Chase the way you did yesterday. It was extremely funny. I heard you, and I heard you searching the dictionary for the difficult words, then swearing because you couldn’t read the definitions!”

The young man plainly thought it unfair to be mocked for his ignorance, then mocked again for trying to overcome it. I thought much the same. Remembering Mrs. Dean’s account of his first attempt to dispel the darkness in which he had been raised, I remarked, “But, Mrs. Heathcliff, we all had to begin, and we all stumbled and faltered at first. If our teachers had mocked us instead of helping, we’d still be stumbling and faltering.”

“Oh! I don’t want to limit his learning,” she replied. “But he has no right to take what’s mine and make it ridiculous to me with his horrible mistakes and mispronunciations! Those books, the prose and the poetry alike, are sacred to me because of other memories. I hate hearing them degraded and profaned in his mouth! And out of everything he could choose, he’s picked my favourite passages, the ones I most love to repeat, as though deliberately to spite me.”

For a minute Hareton’s chest heaved in silence. His humiliation and anger were intense, and he struggled to control them. With a gentleman’s wish to ease his embarrassment, I got up and stood in the doorway, looking outside. He followed my example and left the room, but soon returned with half a dozen books. He flung them into Catherine’s lap, exclaiming, “Take them! I never want to hear them, read them, or think of them again!”
“I don’t want them now,” she answered. “They’ll remind me of you, and I’ll hate them.”

She opened one that had clearly been much handled and read a passage in a beginner’s slow, dragging voice. Then she laughed and threw it away. “And listen to this,” she went on tauntingly, beginning a verse of an old ballad in the same manner.

But his pride could bear no more torment. I heard a blow silence her insolent tongue, and I did not entirely disapprove. The little wretch had done everything she could to wound her cousin’s sensitive, though uncultivated, feelings. Physical force was the only argument he had to settle the account and return some of the hurt to the person who had inflicted it. Afterwards he gathered the books and threw them into the fire. His face showed the anguish of that sacrifice to anger. As they burned, I imagined him remembering the pleasure they had already given him, and the triumph and ever greater pleasures he had expected from them. I thought I could also guess what had prompted his secret studies. Until Catherine crossed his path, he had been content with daily labour and coarse, physical pleasures. Shame at her contempt and hope of winning her approval had first stirred him towards higher things. Instead of protecting him from the first and winning him the second, his efforts to improve himself had achieved precisely the opposite.
“Yes, that’s all a brute like you can get out of them!” Catherine cried, sucking her injured lip and watching the blaze with angry eyes.
“You’d _better_ keep quiet now,” he answered fiercely.

He was too agitated to say more. He hurried towards the doorway, where I stepped aside for him. But before he had crossed the threshold, Mr. Heathcliff met him coming up the paved path, laid a hand on his shoulder, and asked, “What’s the matter now, lad?”
“Nowt, nowt,” he said, breaking away to indulge his grief and anger alone.
Heathcliff watched him go and sighed.

“It would be strange if I defeated myself,” he muttered, unaware that I stood behind him. “But when I look for his father in his face, I find more of _her_ every day! How the devil can he be so like her? I can hardly bear to look at him.”

He lowered his eyes and went gloomily inside. His face had a restless, anxious expression I had never seen before, and he looked thinner. His daughter-in-law had spotted him through the window and immediately escaped to the kitchen, leaving me alone.

“I’m glad to see you out again, Mr. Lockwood,” he said in answer to my greeting. “Partly for selfish reasons. In this wilderness I don’t think I could easily find someone to replace you. More than once I’ve wondered what brought you here.”

“An idle whim, I’m afraid, sir,” I replied. “Or else it’s an idle whim that’s about to carry me away. I leave for London next week, and I must warn you that I have no wish to keep Thrushcross Grange beyond the twelve months I agreed to rent it. I don’t think I shall live there again.”

“Indeed! Tired of exile from the world, are you?” he said. “But if you’ve come to ask to be excused from paying for a house you won’t occupy, you’ve wasted your journey. I never let anyone off what they owe me.”
“I’ve come to ask for no such thing!” I exclaimed, thoroughly irritated. “If you wish, I’ll settle with you now.” I took my notebook from my pocket.

“No, no,” he replied coolly. “If you don’t come back, you’ll leave enough behind to cover your debts. I’m in no hurry. Sit down and have dinner with us. A guest who can be relied on not to return is generally welcome. Catherine! Bring the things in. Where are you?”
Catherine came back carrying a tray of knives and forks.
“You can eat with Joseph,” Heathcliff muttered to her aside, “and stay in the kitchen until he’s gone.”
She followed his instructions exactly. Perhaps she felt no temptation to disobey. Living among boors and people who hate mankind, she probably cannot appreciate better company when she encounters it.

With Mr. Heathcliff grim and gloomy on one side and Hareton entirely silent on the other, I ate a rather cheerless meal and took my leave early. I would have gone out the back way for a final glimpse of Catherine and the pleasure of annoying old Joseph. But Hareton was told to bring my horse round, and my host himself escorted me to the front door, thwarting my intention.

“How drearily life passes in that house!” I reflected as I rode down the road. “What a fulfilment of something more romantic than a fairy tale it would have been for Mrs. Linton Heathcliff if she and I had fallen in love, as her good nurse wished, and gone off together into the lively atmosphere of town!”
